# We’ve Filed More Than 50 Legal Claims Over Abuse by Federal Immigration Agents. Here's Why.


The claimants detail being unlawfully detained, denied medical care, or targeted simply for speaking out or recording what they saw. Their experiences reveal a dangerous pattern of abuse that threatens the rights and safety of us all.


[Yasmin Cader](https://www.aclu.org/bios/yasmin-cader) ,
she/her


,
ACLU


**Share This Page**


August 5, 2026


In April, ICE held one mother, who was five months pregnant, with her husband and four children, including her 11-month-old baby, in a cell with no sunlight and little access to running water for nearly a month. The mother lost consciousness twice from the heat before anyone took her seriously.


“My children were confused and scared about why they were trapped in this cell, why they could not go outside, and why they had no toys to play with,” said the mother, who is unnamed here due to her immigration status.


On July 29, ACLU affiliates announced the filing of 54 federal tort claims against the federal government on behalf of people and families harmed by federal immigration agents across 17 states and Washington, D.C. Like the story of the pregnant mother, each claim reveals the story of someone whose rights were violated by federal law enforcement since President Donald Trump took office again. Some were seriously injured, while others were unlawfully detained, denied medical care, or targeted simply for speaking out or recording what they saw. Together, their experiences reveal a dangerous and widespread pattern of abuse that threatens the rights and safety of us all.

### The People v. Agents of Chaos and Cruelty


Since President Trump took office again, immigration agents have terrorized communities in workplaces, schools and neighborhoods across the country. Masked agents have smashed car windows and dragged people from their vehicles, separated parents from their children, ignored documents proving lawful immigration status, and detained people in dangerous facilities without urgently needed medical care. U.S. citizens and noncitizens alike have been detained, and in some cases, assaulted based on nothing more than how they look or sound. The Trump administration has also targeted U.S. citizens for simply exercising their First Amendment rights and speaking out against federal agents’ abuses.


The consequences of this violence and abuse have been devastating. Many people have suffered serious injuries and property damage, and some have lost their lives. In January, ICE shot and killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. Months later, federal agents shot and killed two men in July: Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine. More than 50 people have also died in ICE detention since the start of President Trump’s mass deportation campaign.


## What’s a Federal Tort Claim?


Such abuses are widespread and systemic, reflecting a coordinated effort to intimidate and control our communities. They require a coordinated response. That’s why the ACLU and our affiliates are taking legal action under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA).


The[Federal Tort Claims Act](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45732) allows a person to seek financial compensation from the federal government if a federal employee hurts them while on the job. Filing a claim is the first step people need to take before they can have their day in court. Without the FTCA, the government would be almost entirely shielded from lawsuits for monetary damages. It is one of the few paths available for someone harmed by a federal agent to hold the government financially accountable, even when the individual officer is never identified or disciplined. We’re using the FTCA to seek accountability and compensation for the abuse our clients experienced at the government’s hands.


## The People Behind Our Campaign Against Federal Immigration Abuses


The 54 stories at the center of this campaign paint a horrifying picture of the terror that federal agents have inflicted on our communities.


In one case, armed, masked agents surrounded Willy Wender Aceituno, a U.S. citizen from North Carolina, outside a restaurant and forced to prove his citizenship. After Aceituno showed the officers identification confirming his citizenship, the officers walked away — only to return minutes later to smash his car window and throw him onto broken glass. They handcuffed Aceituno, placed him in an unmarked SUV, and eventually left him bleeding on the side of the road, miles from his car.

In another case in Vermont, ICE agents broke into José Estrada Jerez’s home in search of a man who was not there and whom Estrada Jerez did not know. The agents violently handcuffed and pointed loaded firearms at him — a U.S. citizen who was only 18 years old at the time.


Together, these stories show that no one is safe from the violence of this administration’s lawless agenda — regardless of immigration status or U.S. citizenship.


## What We’re Fighting For


Filing these claims won’t undo the harm and trauma that our affiliates’ clients endured. No settlement or court judgment can erase what it felt like to be thrown to the ground, separated from your children, or locked in a cell without access to the outside world. But these claims can bring a measure of justice to the people and families affected and help hold the federal government financially accountable for the harm caused.


We’re not stopping there. We need additional pathways to accountability so that justice is accessible to the tens of thousands of people with stories just like those of our claimants. While we’re fighting in court, we’re also[asking Congress](https://action.aclu.org/send-message/keep-our-communities-safe-hold-federal-agents-accountable) to address barriers that allow federal agents to evade responsibility: such as, the near-total lack of a clear path to sue federal agents directly, and, when such a claim is available, qualified immunity, a legal doctrine that can shield officers from liability. We’re also supporting legislation that would bring independent oversight to detention facilities and end family detention.


This is a fight we intend to win. We will use every legal and legislative tool at our disposal to end this abuse, defend people’s rights, and hold the federal government accountable under the law.[Learn more](https://www.aclu.org/campaigns-initiatives/the-people-v-agents-of-chaos-and-cruelty) about the clients ACLU affiliates are representing.

### Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha


The Supreme Court will hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, stemming from our lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s unlawful policy that subjects millions of immigrants to mandatory detention without access to bond hearings. Mandatory detention has played a key role in this administration’s cruel and lawless campaign of mass deportations. This case will decide whether the government can upend how our laws have been understood and applied for decades to lock up millions of immigrants without a chance to show there is no justification for their detention while they fight their removal. The American Civil Liberties Union, New York Civil Liberties Union, Law Office of Paul O’Dwyer, Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, and MacArthur Justice Center are counsel in this case. Oral argument is expected in late February or early March 2027.

### Immigrants’ Rights Organizations File Lawsuit to Stop ICE from Hiding Locations of Detained People


BOSTON — A group of legal services organizations today filed a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s new policy of hiding the locations of thousands of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The policy unlawfully interferes with communication between detainees, their families, and their lawyers. The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the new policy unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients. For over 16 years, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has made the location of detained noncitizens available via its Online Detainee Locator System. In September, DHS abruptly changed course and stopped sharing the location of detained people with final orders of removal, either via the locator service or in direct response to queries from family members or attorneys. This policy of mass disappearance has thrown thousands into an administrative black box without any justification. The new policy facilitates the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign by making it more difficult to provide detainees with access to attorneys and the judicial system — and thus more difficult to challenge unlawful detention and pursue lawful pathways to remain in the United States. Noncitizens with final orders of removal may still pursue a number of legal remedies to challenge their detention and deportation — but if they cannot access legal counsel or the courts, they may never have a chance to seek these remedies before they are deported. The lawsuit alleges that ICE’s implementation of this new policy is arbitrary and capricious, and thus a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The complaint also alleges that ICE’s policy violates the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights. Finally, the complaint alleges violations of the Freedom of Information Act because the government failed to publish details of their new policy. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the new policy, and will shortly file a motion to stay the new policy while their case proceeds. The plaintiffs are represented by the National Immigration Law Center, National Immigration Project, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Massachusetts, and Annelise Araujo Law. The following are statements from the plaintiffs and their legal counsel: Attorneys representing the plaintiffs: “The Trump administration’s new policy of mass disappearance should send a chill through everybody’s spine. By choosing to hide even the most basic information about thousands of people in its custody, the government is unlawfully blocking their access to legal counsel and the courts, and keeping desperate loved ones in the dark. This shockingly malicious policy was implemented suddenly, without any legal basis or justification, and with immediate, devastating impacts for our clients and the people they serve. The government must reverse course immediately, restore the Online Detainee Locator System, and stop hiding people in its vast network of detention facilities.” Jacquelynne J. Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services: “No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them. Even with representation, navigating the legal system is complex for immigrants facing deportation. This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.” Jackie Kelley, director of immigration legal services at the Rian Immigrant Center: “We cannot allow the United States government to indefinitely disappear human beings. If we cannot locate our clients, we cannot pursue the relief for which they are legally eligible. The law gives our clients the right to seek protection. This policy obstructs that right when our clients need it most.” Laura St. John, legal director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project: “The Trump administration is disappearing people within the immigration detention system. This should terrify every single one of us. Thousands of people are no longer being shown on the online detainee locator system, making it impossible for attorneys to locate their clients or identify people who might need emergency legal assistance. How can people in detention possibly have access to due process and safety if there is no way for their families or advocates to know where they are being held?” Aimee Mayer-Salins, deputy program director of legal coordination at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights: “When someone you love is in ICE custody, they shouldn’t simply disappear into a black hole. Families deserve to know where their loved ones are being held, and this lawsuit is about protecting that basic right.” For more information about Greater Boston Legal Services et al. v. Mullin, visit: https://www.aclu.org/cases/greater-boston-legal-services-et-al-v-mullin
